clue.text: Repeatedly bear ridicule

wordplay.note: Winnie-the-Pooh is the famous bear of A. A. Milne's books, and repeatedly means his name appears twice

explanation.surface: Someone keeps having to put up with mockery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bear' looks like a verb meaning endure, but it is a noun: the bear is Pooh, written twice.
explanation.definitionFit: To pooh-pooh an idea is to dismiss it scornfully, which is a synonym for mocking it.

clue.text: Editor in charge limited by pedant, who provides low-level care?

definitions.note: a descriptive phrase standing for the person

indicators.note: something limited by another thing is hemmed in on both sides, so these letters sit inside the other word

parts.note: a purist insists on strict correctness, as a pedant does
ED is the standard abbreviation for editor
IC is short for in charge

explanation.surface: A fussy editor in charge offers care of a rather lowly kind.
explanation.walkthrough: The low level is the feet, which is why the definition ends in a question mark: the care is literally at ground level.
explanation.definitionFit: A pedicurist treats feet and toenails, the lowest part of the body, so the care given is literally low-level.

clue.text: Doubly wrong about charge in a pig-headed way

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the jumbled letters wrap around the next word
a word that has gone wrong is out of order, so its letters must be rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, as anagram fodder
a rate is a charge or fee

explanation.surface: Someone doubly mistaken about a fee carries on stubbornly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Doubly' reads as an adverb modifying wrong, but it is the word to be rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Obdurately means stubbornly refusing to change one's mind, which is what pig-headed describes.

clue.text: Lots of certain animals in containers

definitions.meaning: first meaning: groups of wolves or hounds
second meaning: boxes or bags for carrying things

explanation.surface: Many animals are being kept in boxes.
explanation.definitionFit: Wolves and hounds hunt in packs, and a pack is also a packet or bag that holds goods.

clue.text: Is not Dr Tooth possibly an alias for one?

definitions.text: Is not Dr Tooth possibly an alias for one?

indicators.note: possibly suggests one of several arrangements, so the letters before it may be reordered

parts.note: taken as written, as anagram fodder

explanation.surface: A jokey suggestion that a dentist-type specialist would be nicknamed Dr Tooth.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both the wordplay and the definition: the one who might be called Dr Tooth is a specialist in straightening teeth.
explanation.definitionFit: An orthodontist is a dental specialist who corrects teeth, so Dr Tooth would be a fitting nickname.

clue.text: Tail is part of one and one is part of tail

definitions.text: Tail is part of one and one is part of tail

parts.note: surface reading: an animal has a tail as one of its body parts
setter's reading: in cricket the tail is the weak lower-order batsmen, and a hopeless batsman is called by the name of a small burrowing animal

explanation.surface: A riddle about something that both has a tail and belongs to one.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket the tail is the end of the batting order where the poor batsmen go, and a very poor batsman is nicknamed after the same fluffy-tailed creature.
explanation.definitionFit: The animal has a tail, and in cricket slang the same name means an inept batsman found in the team's tail.

clue.text: Addict across street, right? It's less clear

indicators.note: a word lying across another spans it, so it sits outside and encloses the following letters

parts.note: a substance abuser is an addict
ST is the abbreviation for street
R is short for right

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether an addict is on the right side of the street, and admits it's hazy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Addict across street' reads as a location, but across is the signal to wrap the addict around the next two pieces together.
explanation.definitionFit: Abstruse means obscure and hard to understand, so the comparative form means harder to grasp.

clue.text: Asinine pronouncement from monarch borne by horse

indicators.note: something borne by a carrier is held within it, so the first letter goes inside the second word

parts.note: a bay is a reddish-brown horse
R stands for Rex or Regina, king or queen

explanation.surface: A foolish statement from a king carried on horseback.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Asinine' usually means stupid, but here it is literal: belonging to an ass.
explanation.definitionFit: A bray is the loud cry of a donkey, so it is literally an ass's utterance.

clue.text: Draws, we hear, little piggies for children

indicators.note: we hear means the clue is concerned with how a word sounds when spoken rather than its spelling

parts.note: to tow is to draw or pull along

explanation.surface: Pulls along little pigs for children.
explanation.walkthrough: The nursery rhyme 'This little piggy went to market' is counted on a child's toes, so piggies is the nursery word.
explanation.definitionFit: Children's rhyme calls each digit of the foot a little piggy, so the nursery name stands for these.

clue.text: Awful deed, act I commit

indicators.note: awful suggests something botched and messy, so the following letters are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written, as anagram fodder

explanation.surface: A criminal confesses to a terrible act.
explanation.definitionFit: To dedicate yourself to a cause is to commit to it, so the two verbs are synonyms.

clue.text: Land in country, European nation

parts.note: E is short for European
a state is a nation

explanation.surface: A list of places: a rural area, a European nation.
explanation.definitionFit: An estate is a large area of land and property in the countryside, owned by one person.

clue.text: People using crooks with little money, namely to get something to eat

parts.note: shepherds carry crooks, hooked staffs
P is a penny, a small coin
i.e. stands for id est, that is or namely

explanation.surface: Criminals use a little cash to buy food.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crooks' suggests criminals, but these are shepherds' hooked staffs. Shepherd's pie is a British dish of minced lamb topped with mashed potato.
explanation.definitionFit: Shepherd's pie is a dish of minced meat and mashed potato, so it is something eaten.

clue.text: Saint seen in awfully rich bar with that woman

indicators.note: awfully suggests something done badly, so the following word's letters are mixed up

parts.note: taken as written, as anagram fodder
to bar is to stop
her refers to that woman

explanation.surface: A saint is spotted in a very swanky pub with a woman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bar' looks like a pub, but here it is the verb meaning prevent.
explanation.definitionFit: St Christopher is the patron saint of travellers, so the name stands for a saint.

clue.text: Removing skin around swelling, as form of prepping

indicators.note: around means surrounding, so the first word wraps around the second

parts.note: paring is peeling the skin off fruit or vegetables
a boil is an inflamed swelling on the skin

explanation.surface: Peeling the skin round an inflamed lump, as part of getting ready.
explanation.definitionFit: Parboiling is partly boiling food before finishing it another way, a common step in preparing a dish.

clue.text: Exerted control about accommodation and raised prices again

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the first word goes around the next

parts.note: to rein in a horse is to control it
a flat is an apartment, a place to live

explanation.surface: A landlord tightened his grip on housing and put up the rents once more.
explanation.definitionFit: Inflation is a rise in prices, so reinflated means pushed prices up again.

clue.text: Produces text, we hear, about donkey in part of book — major life events

indicators.note: in places the animal inside the following words, enclosed by them
we hear means the word is identified by its sound rather than its spelling

parts.note: someone who produces text writes
of can mean about, as in 'speak of'
a page is part of a book
an ass is a donkey

explanation.surface: An author writes about a donkey in a chapter of a book covering big life moments.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' looks like the container signal but it gives the word OF; the donkey sits inside the part of a book.
explanation.definitionFit: Rites of passage are ceremonies marking transitions such as birth, coming of age, marriage and death.

clue.text: Internalised moral restraints group sees as distorted

indicators.note: something seen as distorted is warped out of shape, so the letters before it are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, as anagram fodder

explanation.surface: A group regards conscience-driven rules as twisted.
explanation.definitionFit: In Freudian psychology the superego is the part of the mind that holds internalised moral standards and conscience.

clue.text: See 15
Sailor robbed saint, reportedly — part of explosive mixture

parts.note: an old salt is an experienced sailor

indicators.note: reportedly means as said aloud, so a spoken form stands in for the spelling

parts.note: the saying 'rob Peter to pay Paul' makes St Peter the saint who is robbed

explanation.surface: A seaman stole from a saint, the report says, and something explosive is involved.
explanation.walkthrough: The saint who gets robbed comes from the saying 'rob Peter to pay Paul'; the second half sounds like his name.
explanation.definitionFit: Saltpetre, potassium nitrate, is one of the three ingredients of gunpowder with charcoal and sulphur.

clue.text: Burgle home to get bird

parts.note: to burgle is to rob a building
to be in is to be at home

explanation.surface: A thief breaks into a house and makes off with a bird.
explanation.definitionFit: The robin is a small songbird with a red breast, common in British gardens.

clue.text: Accommodating people, like an initially powerless political leader

indicators.note: powerless at the start means the word loses its opening letter, the one standing for power

parts.note: like a president, a political leader; 'like an' turns the noun into an adjective

explanation.surface: A political leader is helpful to people but has lost authority from the start.
explanation.walkthrough: P is the abbreviation for power, so 'powerless' at the start removes the opening P.
explanation.definitionFit: Residential describes a building or area that provides housing, so it accommodates people.

clue.text: Innocent the First dividing part of church

indicators.note: dividing means splitting something in two by going inside it

parts.note: the nave is the main body of a church
I is the Roman numeral one, as in a monarch's regnal number

explanation.surface: Pope Innocent I splitting a section of the church.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Innocent the First' reads as the name of an early pope; Innocent is in fact the definition, and the First is the numeral.
explanation.definitionFit: Naive means unworldly and lacking experience, a synonym for innocent.

clue.text: This German ruler, on reflection, is no different

indicators.note: a word that looks the same when reflected backwards reads identically in both directions

parts.note: this refers to the answer itself, the ruler's name

explanation.surface: A German ruler, thinking it over, has not changed.
explanation.walkthrough: The name reads the same in both directions, which is what 'on reflection, is no different' says.
explanation.definitionFit: Otto the Great was a tenth-century German king and Holy Roman Emperor, so the name fits a ruler.

clue.text: Girl coming to harm following Jack

indicators.note: following says one piece comes after the other in the answer

parts.note: J is the abbreviation for jack in a pack of cards
ill means harm, as in 'wish someone ill'

explanation.surface: The nursery rhyme: Jill fell down after Jack and got hurt.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is Jack and Jill, who went up the hill; Jack fell first and Jill came tumbling after.
explanation.definitionFit: Jill is a girl's name, and in old usage a jill is also a girl or young woman.

clue.text: Prioritise treatment when a tiger runs amok

indicators.note: running amok is going wild and out of control, so the letters are thrown into disorder

parts.note: taken as written, as anagram fodder

explanation.surface: Medics must decide who to treat first after a tiger attack.
explanation.definitionFit: To triage casualties is to sort them by urgency so that the worst injured are treated first.

clue.text: One living in hope as I tip most haphazardly

indicators.note: haphazardly means at random, so the letters are arranged in a new random order

parts.note: taken as written, as anagram fodder

explanation.surface: A gambler stays hopeful while placing random tips.
explanation.definitionFit: An optimist expects things to turn out well, so they live in hope.

clue.text: Wise-looking old learner included in list in the past

parts.note: O is short for old

indicators.note: something included in another is placed inside it

parts.note: list is an archaic verb meaning to wish or desire
L is for learner, as on a learner driver's plate

explanation.surface: An experienced student who once appeared on a list now looks clever.
explanation.walkthrough: 'List' looks like a register of names, but in old English it was a verb meaning to desire, as in 'the wind bloweth where it listeth'.
explanation.definitionFit: Owls are traditionally symbols of wisdom, so owlish describes someone looking solemn and wise.

clue.text: Settled score with duke, say, at no point retreating

indicators.note: retreating means going backwards, so the whole string is read from the end

parts.note: D is short for duke
e.g., for example, is what 'say' means in 'a fruit, say'
at no point in time means never

explanation.surface: A duke got even, never once backing down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Duke, say' looks like an example of a nobleman, but 'say' is its own piece meaning for example.
explanation.definitionFit: To revenge a wrong is to get back at the wrongdoer, which is what settling a score means.
